activities.anchor: how tightly do the particles cling to each other
activities.caption: file each behaviour by the state it belongs to
activities.name: somClingSort

config.prompt: Seven behaviours, three states — file each into the state that does it:

items.label: locked into an ordered lattice, only vibrating
in contact but free to slide past each other
flying freely through mostly empty space
keeps its own shape without a container
keeps a fixed volume but adopts the container's shape
pushes on every wall with pressure
can be squeezed into a smaller volume

config.why: Grip strength decides everything: locked in place, sliding in contact, or flying free — added heat walks a substance down the row.

activities.caption: pair each claim with the observation that backs it
activities.name: somPredMatch

config.prompt: Pair each claim with the observation behind it:

pairs.left: a gas is a thousand times less dense than its liquid
pairs.right: same particles, different spacing — water vapour is about 1/1,700 the density of liquid water
heat can only crawl by vibration there; mobile carriers are needed to carry it by travelling
N₂ and O₂ at 28 and 32 g/mol are chunkier than water's 18 — the molecules are few and far between, not small

pairs.left: a steel ball expands in a flame
pairs.right: the iron atoms stay the same size — what grows is the spacing between them

config.why: Spacing, not particle size: one story covers density, conduction limits and expansion.

activities.anchor: Reorganising the solid lattice into a liquid
activities.caption: call the energy bill for turning water to vapour
activities.name: somLatentEst

config.prompt: One gram of water, already at 100 °C — roughly how much energy does turning it fully to vapour take?
config.why: About 2,260 J/g, versus 334 J/g to melt ice — pulling particles fully apart breaks far more attractions than merely loosening their grip.
config.context: A steam burn is worse than a boiling-water burn because condensing hands this energy to skin; each gram of evaporating sweat carries it away at the same rate.

activities.caption: slide to the boiling point where the air is thin
activities.name: somEverestPlace

config.prompt: At the top of the world's highest mountain, air pressure is roughly a third of sea level. Slide the marker to water's boiling point there.
config.why: The answer is about 71 °C — the vapour has to match only a third of the outside push. Double the push in a pressure cooker and the boil climbs to about 121 °C: hotter water, not harder water.

activities.caption: find the faulty line — the route below the triple point
activities.name: somSubSpot

config.prompt: A summary of the phase map contains one faulty line — click it:
lines: Every point of a phase diagram is one pressure–temperature pair; the region it lands in is the state taken there.
The two boundary lines meet at the triple point — for water, 0.01 °C and 611 Pa — where all three phases coexist stably.
That fixed reference is where the kelvin scale is defined from.
Below the triple-point pressure there is no liquid, so ice must melt first and then evaporate — two steps, never one.
Dry ice smokes and vanishes at atmospheric pressure because its triple point lies far above what air can supply.
config.correction: Below the triple point there is no liquid lane at all: ice goes straight to vapour — sublimation, the route Martian frost and shrinking freezer cubes take.
config.why: No liquid lane survives below the crossing, so the solid-to-vapour route needs no intermediate step.

activities.caption: true or false — reading the heating curve
activities.name: somCurveJudge

statements.s: While ice melts at 0 °C, the energy poured in is ungluing the lattice, not raising the temperature.
statements.why: Latent heat: 334 J/g spent ungluing, so the thermometer stays pinned until the last cube is gone.

statements.s: The boil is the shortest flat step on the curve because vapour warms fastest.
statements.why: It is the longest step — 2,260 J/g, since separating particles completely breaks far more attractions than melting does.

statements.s: A pure substance freezes at a single sharp temperature; a mixture slides through a range.
statements.why: That is why a melting point is a standard identity and purity check in every chemistry lab.

statements.s: Water's specific heat of 4.2 J/g per °C is unusually low, so liquid water warms very quickly.
statements.why: It is unusually HIGH — another signature property of water, which is why the liquid rise on the curve is a gentle slope.

activities.anchor: The warming bike pump and the sealed can bursting on a stove
activities.caption: fill the blanks — one story told twice
activities.name: somGasCloze

config.text: Squeeze a gas into a smaller box and its %%0%% climbs — the same number of collisions now landing on less %%1%%. Warm it at fixed volume and the particles hit %%2%% and more often.
config.hint: Pressure is nothing but collisions with the wall — fewer walls of space means more hits per second.

activities.anchor: the ring forms about 1.45× closer to the heavier gas
activities.caption: which curve tracks diffusion rate against mass?
activities.name: somDiffTrace

config.prompt: Diffusion rate plotted against particle mass at fixed temperature — which curve is right?

curves.label: curve A — falls toward big masses

config.why: Lighter particles move faster at the same temperature — ammonia (17 g/mol) outruns hydrogen chloride (36.5 g/mol), so the white ammonium-chloride ring sits about 1.45× nearer the slow one.
